design_detail: RETRACTED PRIMATE REPORT, CARDED AS A RECORD ONLY (METHODS §3.2). Science 2002;297:2260-2263, retracted on 12 September 2003 (the publisher's PDF carries the line 'Retracted 12 September 2003; see last page'). The brief for this batch asked for a card of design 'commentary'; the schema's design list has no such value and the validator's narrative group contains it, so 'narrative-review' is used, as for the retraction notices already carded, and the choice is flagged for the senior author's open decision on a design for notices and withdrawn records (SENIOR-DECISIONS item 29(5)). What the report described: squirrel monkeys and baboons given three doses of 2 mg/kg of what the authors believed was MDMA at 3-hour intervals (subcutaneously in squirrel monkeys, intramuscularly in baboons), then examined 2 to 8 weeks later for brain serotonin and dopamine markers, with silver staining and glial staining in two animals and a dopamine-depletion challenge in three. The retraction notice (Ricaurte et al., 2003) states that the drug given to all but one animal was methamphetamine, so the report is a record of what was claimed, never evidence about MDMA.
can_establish: Nothing about MDMA. The card records what the 2002 report claimed, which dose regimen it described, how many animals died or did not complete it, and the public-health conclusions it drew, so that the claim about the retraction can state what was withdrawn.
cannot_establish: Any effect of MDMA on dopamine or serotonin systems in primates or people: the compound given to all but one animal was methamphetamine, as the authors reported a year later. The report also cannot establish which animal received MDMA or what that animal showed, since the notice does not say.

sample.recruitment: Laboratory animals (Saimiri sciureus and Papio anubis) at Johns Hopkins; no further detail given.
sample.demographics: Species only; sex, age and weight are not given in the report text (they may be in the supporting online material, which was not read).
sample.attrition: Of 5 squirrel monkeys, 1 developed malignant hyperthermia and died within hours of the last dose and 1 received only 2 of the 3 doses after becoming unsteady; of 5 baboons, 1 died after only 2 doses, with hyperthermia up to 41.6 C named as an important factor, and 1 more received only 2 doses. So 2 of 10 animals given the regimen died and 2 others did not complete it.
sample.selection_effects: Not applicable; the decisive problem is the compound given, not the sampling.

exposure.measurement: None of the kind the encyclopedia records: the compound was taken from a bottle labelled MDMA, and the laboratory discovered a year later that it contained methamphetamine (Ricaurte et al., 2003).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: As described in the report: 2 mg/kg three times at 3-hour intervals, total 6 mg/kg, subcutaneous in squirrel monkeys and intramuscular in baboons. The report argued that these doses, adjusted with interspecies scaling, were lower than those typically taken by people (1.6 to 2.4 mg/kg).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Animals were examined 3.5 days (staining), 2 weeks or 6 to 8 weeks after dosing.

comparison.controls: Saline-treated animals of each species (3 squirrel monkeys, 3 baboons).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-dosing measurement in the same animals; all comparisons are between treated and saline-treated animals.

outcomes.instruments: Regional brain serotonin, 5-HIAA, serotonin transporter, dopamine, DOPAC, dopamine transporter and vesicular monoamine transporter by neurochemistry and quantitative autoradiography; immunoreactive axon counts; silver staining for degenerating terminals; glial fibrillary acidic protein staining; a motor challenge with a dopamine-synthesis blocker in 3 animals.
outcomes.operationalization: Neurotoxicity operationalized as lasting reductions in axonal markers plus argyrophilic debris and a glial response.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: One-way analysis of variance followed by individual comparisons; no correction described in the report text.

analysis.effect_sizes: As reported for the animal that received only two doses, 6 weeks later: caudate dopamine -65%, DOPAC -77%, dopamine transporter -51%; serotonin -37%, 5-HIAA -48%, serotonin transporter -40%. Group means are shown only in figures, which are images and were not read. No effect on noradrenaline markers was reported. These figures describe animals given methamphetamine and are recorded here only as what the report stated.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not assessable; the report is four pages with most data in figures and a supporting online file that was not read.
analysis.power: Not reported; groups of 3 to 5 animals.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Nothing about MDMA. On the report's own terms it described large reductions in striatal dopamine markers and smaller reductions in serotonin markers in 2 species after 3 doses of a compound believed to be MDMA, with 2 of 10 animals dying during dosing.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The report concluded that people who take repeated doses over several hours are at high risk of severe brain dopamine injury, that this may put them at increased risk of parkinsonism and other disorders later in life, and that cognitive problems reported in people who use ecstasy may be related to dopaminergic rather than serotonergic toxicity. It also argued that oral use offers little protection and that the doses used were, after interspecies scaling, lower than those people take, a statement that the same authors contradicted in their 2003 reply to critics, where they wrote that interspecies scaling had not been used in these studies (see card sc_mithoefer_2003).

timeline.event: Publication in Science on 27 September 2002, with national press coverage of the claim that one night's use could cause brain damage
Published criticism in Science (6 June) that the high mortality showed the regimen was not a common recreational one, with the authors' reply

Retraction on 12 September 2003: the authors report that all but one animal received methamphetamine from a mislabelled bottle, and that their own attempts to reproduce the dopamine finding with authenticated MDMA had failed
Review of molecular imaging finds no consistent dopamine effect of MDMA in people

replication.where_it_stands: Retracted and never replicated. Under METHODS §3.2 it is cited only to document the retraction; the dopamine question in people is treated in the claim on human dopamine markers.

funding.funder: US Public Health Service grants DA 5707, DA 13790, DA 09487, DA 00206 and DA 10217 (Acknowledgements, p. 2263).
funding.affiliations_note: Departments of Neurology, Neurosciences and Psychiatry, Johns Hopkins; the same laboratory produced the 1998 and 2005 human PET studies of the serotonin transporter.

what_would_settle_it: Nothing can repair this report. The underlying question, whether dose regimens resembling human use damage dopamine neurons in primates, would need a new study with authenticated drug, independent verification of the compound and blinded outcome assessment.

domains.note: Not a review; the item is read here as whether the document can be used as a source of evidence at all, and it cannot: it is retracted.
The report's central exposure was never verified; the compound given was established only after publication, by analysis of frozen brains and of the bottle's contents.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The argument for human relevance rests on the same laboratory's earlier primate work and on an interspecies scaling claim the authors later said they had not used.
The conclusions about parkinsonism in people and about cognitive problems being dopaminergic are speculation presented as implications of the findings.

domains.domain: Balance of the account of human relevance (the risks of the regimen are under-represented)
domains.note: Two of ten animals died and two more could not complete the regimen, yet the regimen is described as one commonly used by people.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No instrument is appropriate: the paper is retracted and is read only as a record of what was claimed (METHODS §3.2). The editors' narrative-review checklist is used as the schema's closest available device, with its domains read as questions about the document as a record. It may be cited only by the claim that documents the retraction.

key_findings.finding: The regimen described was 2 mg/kg three times at 3-hour intervals, a total of 6 mg/kg, given subcutaneously to squirrel monkeys and intramuscularly to baboons, and presented as modelling a regimen used by people at all-night dance parties.

Of 5 squirrel monkeys, 1 died of malignant hyperthermia within hours of the last dose and 1 received only 2 doses after becoming unsteady; of 5 baboons, 1 died after 2 doses, with hyperthermia up to 41.6 C named as an important factor, and 1 more received only 2 doses.
key_findings.note: So 2 of the 10 animals given the regimen died. The authors' 2003 reply to critics stated that one of ten monkeys had died (card sc_mithoefer_2003); the report itself describes two deaths in two species.

key_findings.finding: The report claimed lasting reductions in brain serotonin, 5-HIAA and the serotonin transporter, and a larger loss of striatal dopamine markers, with the animal that received only two doses showing caudate dopamine -65%, DOPAC -77% and dopamine transporter -51% at 6 weeks, alongside serotonin -37%, 5-HIAA -48% and serotonin transporter -40%.
key_findings.note: These figures describe animals that, as the 2003 notice states, received methamphetamine; they are recorded only as what the report claimed.

key_findings.finding: Silver staining 3.5 days after dosing was reported to show argyrophilic debris characteristic of terminal degeneration in the striatum, with a glial response in adjacent sections, and no such debris in a control animal; noradrenaline markers were reported unaffected in both species.

The report concluded that people who use repeated doses over several hours are at high risk of severe brain dopaminergic injury, that this could put them at increased risk of parkinsonism later in life, and that cognitive problems in people who use ecstasy might be dopaminergic rather than serotonergic in origin.
The report argued that the individual doses used were lower than those people typically take (1.6 to 2.4 mg/kg) once adjusted by interspecies dose scaling, citing a pharmacokinetics text.
key_findings.note: In the 2003 exchange in Science the same authors replied to critics that interspecies scaling had not been used in these studies; the two statements cannot both be right.

reporting_issues.issue: The compound given was not verified before publication; the identity of the drug is the one measurement on which everything in the report depends.
reporting_issues.consequence: The report is retracted; nothing in it bears on MDMA.

reporting_issues.issue: A regimen that killed 2 of 10 animals and that 2 more could not complete is described as modelling a dose regimen commonly used by people.
reporting_issues.consequence: The mortality is reported in the text but not carried into the conclusions, and it was the first point the published critics raised (card sc_mithoefer_2003).

reporting_issues.issue: The claim that the doses were lower than human doses after interspecies scaling conflicts with the authors' later statement that interspecies scaling was not used.
reporting_issues.consequence: The human-relevance argument in the report cannot be reconciled with the authors' own later account.

reporting_issues.issue: Group data appear almost entirely in figures, with numbers given in the text only for the single animal that received two doses.
reporting_issues.consequence: Even setting the retraction aside, the report's quantitative claims could not be checked from the text; figures were not read for values here.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 2260-2263 (the full report text; figures are images and no values were read from them; the supporting online material was not read)
